title: Dustin Poirier Calls on Michael Chandler to Retire After Brutal Four-Fight Losing Streak
excerpt: The retired former UFC interim champion says his old rival is taking too much damage and questions what Chandler is still fighting for at 40.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dustin Poirier urges Michael Chandler to retire, questioning his continued fighting at age 40.
  • Chandler is on a four-fight losing streak, with three losses by stoppage.
  • Poirier retired in 2025 due to brain health concerns, mirroring his worries for Chandler.
  • Chandler's recent record is 1-6 over the last seven fights in five years.
  • Dustin Poirier said on the Deep Waters podcast that Michael Chandler should retire, asking "what are we doing?" about his former rival's continued fighting.
  • Chandler, 40, is on a four-fight losing streak with three defeats by stoppage, including a first-round TKO loss to Mauricio Ruffy at UFC Freedom 250 in June.
  • Poirier, who retired in 2025 citing brain health concerns, questioned Chandler's reported plan to move up to welterweight.
  • Chandler has gone 1-6 in his last seven fights over five years but has not indicated any intention to retire.

Dustin Poirier has never been one to hold back, and retirement has not softened that instinct. The former UFC interim lightweight champion used an appearance on the Deep Waters podcast to deliver a blunt message to his old rival Michael Chandler: it is time to stop fighting.

"With all due respect, we buried the hatchet and shook hands," Poirier said. "But Michael Chandler, what are we doing?"

A Losing Streak and Mounting Damage

The question is pointed because the numbers are damning. Chandler, 40, has lost four consecutive fights, with three of those defeats coming by stoppage. His most recent appearance, at the high-profile UFC Freedom 250 card at the White House in June, ended in a first-round TKO at the hands of Brazilian rising star Mauricio Ruffy. Over his last seven bouts spanning five years, the former Bellator champion has managed just one victory.

Poirier, who retired from MMA in 2025 after losing the BMF title fight to Max Holloway, said his own decision to step away was driven partly by concern over brain health — the same concern he now has for Chandler.

"If 155ers are stopping you and you're taking all this damage, what are 170ers going to do? He's too short. He's not long enough. I want to know what he's fighting for?"

— Dustin Poirier

Poirier was responding to reports that Chandler is considering a move up to welterweight, a 170-pound division populated by larger, longer fighters. At 5-foot-8 with a 69-inch reach, Chandler would face a significant size disadvantage against most welterweight contenders.

The White House Card and What Came After

Many observers expected the UFC Freedom 250 loss to be Chandler's final fight. The event carried the symbolic weight of a historic UFC card hosted at the White House, and a retirement announcement would have given Chandler a dignified exit. Instead, the Missouri native has made no public statements about hanging up his gloves and appears intent on continuing.

That stubbornness is part of what made Chandler a fan favorite during his prime. He arrived in the UFC from Bellator in 2021 with a reputation as one of the most explosive fighters in the sport, knocking out Dan Hooker in his debut and immediately establishing himself as a title contender. His 2022 Fight of the Year performance against Justin Gaethje remains one of the most celebrated bouts in UFC history.

A Complicated Rivalry

Poirier and Chandler share a tangled history. Their fight at UFC 281 in November 2022 ended with a Poirier submission victory, after which "The Diamond" accused Chandler of eye gouging. The verbal sparring continued for years, with Chandler questioning Poirier's career decisions and Poirier dismissing Chandler as an outsider — "You just got here, buddy. You're not one of us."

The two reportedly reconciled while working together on the film Road House 2, and Poirier has acknowledged burying the hatchet. But the retirement call suggests the respect is real even if the delivery remains characteristically unsparing.

Chandler has not responded publicly to Poirier's comments. At 40, with a record that now reads 23-11, the question is whether he can find the fight that justifies continuing — or whether the damage sustained in his recent losing stretch has already answered that question for him.
